title: Input-optimal construction of compact inverse suffix arrays
formal: Do there exist a uniform deterministic construction algorithm \(B\), a uniform deterministic query algorithm \(A\), and constants \(C_B,C_S,C_A>0\), such that for every \(n\ge2\) and every packed binary text \(T\in\{0,1\}^n\), \(B\) constructs a static index in at most \(C_B(1+n/\log_2(n+2))\) worst-case word-RAM steps, the retained index and query workspace together occupy at most \(C_S n\) bits, and \(A\) answers every query \(i\in\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\) with \(\operatorname{ISA}_T[i]\) in at most \(C_A\) worst-case steps? All three constants and the programs are independent of \(n,T,i\). Both algorithms use the common word model specified below.
definitions: The input supplies \(n\) and the consecutive bits of \(T\), packed into words with only the last word padded. \(\operatorname{ISA}_T[i]\) is the zero-based lexicographic rank of \(T[i..n)\) among all nonempty suffixes, with \(0<1\) and shorter proper prefixes first.  Use a uniform sequential word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\), for a fixed integer \(d\ge 8\) chosen with the algorithm. A fixed finite program must handle every input size; there is no advice, precomputed lookup table or input-dependent oracle. Unit-cost operations are reads, writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and integer quotient and remainder for a nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Addresses and stored values fit words; multiword operations pay for their constituent instructions. No random bits are available. All initialization, preprocessing, tables and output writes are charged. A static query starts without input-dependent private state, and every retained copy of the input or auxiliary information counts toward index space. Every bit retained after construction, including the input if retained, counts toward the index. Query work storage is also charged to this bit bound. The construction time includes reading the packed input and writing every index word; no prebuilt instance-dependent structure is supplied. Query outputs are the exact integer rank in \(\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\), written in a word. The query routine has access only to the retained index, the size parameter and its query index. Its input-dependent working state does not persist as an additional uncharged store between queries. Construction workspace need not satisfy a separate linear-bit bound, but allocating, initializing and accessing it consumes the stated construction time. Space is measured in bits of all occupied words, including word padding. Binary input bits have a fixed agreed order within each word, and unused bits of the last word are zero. The logarithmic time bound is the packed-input scale in this word model.

context_blocks.text: The input-optimal construction endpoint is the editorial question approved for this card’s import. It strengthens the sublinear-construction questions discussed in the August 2026 source, which the source itself answers. The stronger endpoint is retained explicitly rather than attributed verbatim to the paper’s numbered questions. Its present openness has not been independently certified.

Kempa and Kociumaka’s August 2026 preprint states a deterministic \(O(n\log_2\sigma)\)-bit inverse suffix-array index with constant worst-case query time and construction time \(O(n\min\{1,\log_2\sigma/\sqrt{\log_2 n}\})\) for alphabet size \(2\le\sigma\le n\). For binary texts this gives \(O(n/\sqrt{\log_2 n})\), which is slower than the card’s \(O(n/\log_2 n)\) endpoint. Theorem 1.1 also bounds peak preprocessing space, an additional property of that result rather than an extra requirement on this card.

The preprint states that improving the construction time below its binary-text bound, while retaining sufficiently fast inverse queries, would improve the known time for Dictionary Matching. That is a conditional connection to another algorithmic task, not an unconditional lower bound excluding this card’s construction target.

Munro, Navarro and Nekrich’s CPM 2020 paper establishes sublinear deterministic construction for a compact text-search index. Its pattern-counting and occurrence-reporting guarantees concern different queries; that result does not itself give the constant-time inverse suffix-array functionality requested here.

why: An inverse suffix-array query identifies the lexicographic position of a suffix without storing all ranks explicitly. A compact index with constant query time would be especially useful if its construction were as fast as processing the packed representation. The remaining construction gap tests a substantive barrier shared with other packed-string tasks.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence assertion or its logical negation. A positive answer must specify both fixed finite programs and prove exact suffix ranks for every binary text and every legal query, the construction bound, the total retained-bit bound and the constant worst-case query bound together. A negative answer must rule out all pairs of programs and all choices of their fixed constants in this model. A conditional lower bound establishes only its conditional implication. Linear space with slower queries, constant queries with more space, or sublinear construction slower than the displayed packed-input bound does not meet the full target.

status_note: Uncertain current status after individual review on 2026-09-15. Bounded later-work searches found no exact resolution but do not independently certify this recent endpoint as open.

importance.reason: Closing the construction gap would make a fundamental compact text index as cheap asymptotically as reading and writing its representation.

category_assignment.reason: The main target is a general string-processing, compressed-representation or sequence-comparison primitive.

sentences: The input is a binary text packed into machine words.
The desired static index must answer the exact lexicographic rank of any suffix in constant worst-case time.
All retained information and query workspace must occupy a linear number of bits.
The question asks whether deterministic construction can take time proportional to the number of packed input words.
An August 2026 preprint has a square-root-logarithmic construction gap and a conditional connection to faster Dictionary Matching, while this stronger endpoint remains status-uncertain.
